question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
**Short answer:** Under the law in force on 1 November 2019, a notice to vacate given in response to you exercising a right under the Act is of no effect. For a no-reason notice, you have 60 days to challenge it at the Tribunal. Whether this notice is retaliatory depends on the reason it states and the timing.

**Which law applies:** The retrieved document is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 088 (file "rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf"), in force from 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). That covers 1 November 2019. The text includes both the older "landlord/tenant" provisions and newer "residential rental provider/renter" provisions, and the documents don't say which applies to a given notice. The sections below are from the older numbering, so check which provisions apply to your tenancy.

**What the law says**

- A notice to vacate under s 263 (no reason given) is of no effect if it was given in response to the tenant exercising a right under the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- A no-reason notice under s 263 must give at least 120 days for "any other tenancy agreement," which would include a periodic one [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- Notices must be in writing, signed, and in the prescribed form. Except for s 263 notices, they must state the reason [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- A tenant can't challenge a s 263 notice after 60 days from the date it is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**What to check**

1. **Which section the notice relies on.** If it gives no reason, it is likely a s 263 notice. The s 263 notice doesn't need a reason, which is why it is often used in retaliation cases [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
2. **The termination date.** For a no-reason notice on a periodic agreement, it must be at least 120 days after the notice date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). If it's shorter, it may be invalid.
3. **Form and signature.** Check that it's in writing, signed by the landlord or their agent, addressed to you, and in the prescribed form [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Timing and causation.** The retaliation test is whether the notice was given "in response to" your exercise of a right [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Your repair request is the right in question. Relevant evidence includes your written repair requests, dates, and any communication from the landlord. The documents don't define "in response to," so I can't tell you how the Tribunal would weigh timing alone.
5. **Written repair notice.** The Act's repair provisions refer to written notice. For example, a renter must give written notice of damage or breakdown of facilities "as soon as practicable" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Also, a non-urgent repair application to the Director requires written notice to the landlord and 14 days without repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Check that your requests were in writing.

**What you can do or ask**

- **Challenge the notice at the Tribunal.** Under s 266(3)(c), a challenge to a s 263 notice must be made within 60 days after the notice date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). For 1 November 2019, that is about **31 December 2019**. Count carefully.
- **Note the 30-day rule for other notices.** Section 321B lets a tenant challenge certain notices (ss 255–260, 285, 286, 310) within 30 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). A s 263 notice is not in that list, so don't rely on the 30-day window for a no-reason notice. If the notice cites another section, check whether the 30-day window applies. That would be 1 December 2019.
- **Be ready for a possession application.** The Tribunal can only issue a possession order if it is satisfied, among other things, that the landlord was entitled to give the notice and the notice has not been withdrawn [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Keep paying rent and staying in the property** until the Tribunal decides, because a possession order requires the tenant to be still in possession after the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover**

- They don't define "in response to" or set out how the Tribunal decides retaliation.
- They don't confirm which version of the renter provisions (for example, s 72AA) was in force on 1 November 2019 or how it applies to your tenancy.
- They don't tell you the exact notice form or whether a prescribed period applies in place of the 120-day period.

For advice on your specific notice, consider contacting a tenant advice service or VCAT directly.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. The answer says a s 263 no-reason notice 'must give at least 120 days for "any other tenancy agreement," which would include a periodic one'. It says such a notice 'is of no effect if it was given in response to the tenant exercising a right under the Act', and identifies the repair request as that right. It also says 'a challenge to a s 263 notice must be made within 60 days after the notice date' at the Tribunal, and refers the tenant to VCAT.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer never says the landlord needed a reason, stating instead that "The s 263 notice doesn't need a reason." It gives the 60-day deadline ("a challenge to a s 263 notice must be made within 60 days after the notice date... about 31 December 2019") and raises the 30-day window only to reject it for this notice ("don't rely on the 30-day window for a no-reason notice").

The answer names the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 088 (file "rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf"), in force from 2 July 2019', which was in force on 1 November 2019. Its core rules (s 263 retaliation and the 120-day period, s 266(3) 60-day challenge window, the 14-day Director repair application) come from that version's operative text. Renter-era provisions such as s 72AA appear only as gaps, not as rules applied to the user.

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents support a challenge on two points: the rental provider's offer of a higher rent, and any false or misleading representation about rent. They do not say anything about a false "withdrawn" record or what evidence to keep, so those parts of your question are not answered by the sources.

The law below is from the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Version 110, which the metadata shows was in force from 6 August 2025 to 24 November 2025, so it covers 1 October 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Advertised rent must be a fixed amount.** A provider or agent must not advertise or offer premises unless the rent is advertised or offered as a fixed amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **No inviting higher offers.** A provider or agent "must not solicit or otherwise invite an offer of an amount of rent that is higher than the advertised amount of rent" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person and 300 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **No false or misleading rent representations.** A provider or agent who promotes or advertises premises "must not make a false or misleading representation in relation to the rent" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). This applies to providers not acting in trade or commerce, and the same penalties apply [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Misleading conduct that induces you to sign.** A provider or agent must not induce a person to enter a residential rental agreement by misleading or deceptive conduct, including a false or misleading representation about "the rent payable under the agreement" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The Act notes that the Tribunal can make orders for contraventions of this section [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

The Act states that a higher-offer invitation is an offence [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Whether a higher offer was actually accepted, and whether the "withdrawn" email was false, would need to be established on the facts. The documents do not address this.

## What you can do or ask

- **Consider a complaint or Tribunal application.** The Act provides for Tribunal orders for contraventions of s 30E [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The documents do not set out a complaint process or time limits for s 30F or s 30G.
- **Seek advice.** The Statement of Information for Rental Applicants lists VCAT (1300 018 228), Victoria Legal Aid (1300 792 387), and VEOHRC (1300 292 153) for discrimination-related help [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Victoria Legal Aid is listed for advice on unlawful discrimination, so it is relevant only if you think the decision involved a protected attribute [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Discrimination.** If you believe the decision was based on a protected attribute such as age, race, or parental status, the Act allows compensation applications to VCAT under s 210AA [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Nothing you described suggests this, so it is only worth pursuing if the facts support it.

## What to save as evidence

The retrieved documents do not list specific evidence to keep. In general, you would want to keep anything that shows the advertised rent, your application, the "withdrawn" email, and the new listing with its higher rent. This is general practice, not something the sources say.

**Limitation:** I could not find anything in the sources about how a withdrawal is recorded, how a rent increase is handled after a listing, or how to lodge a complaint about the higher offer.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not, at least not on the allergy ground alone. The documents say a rental provider must not unreasonably refuse, and a provider who doesn't apply to the Tribunal within 14 days is taken to have consented. Whether the refusal is reasonable is not something the documents resolve for an allergy.

**What the law says**

- A renter may keep a pet only if the provider has consented in writing or the Tribunal has ordered it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- A renter must make the request in the form approved by the Director [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- A provider "must not unreasonably refuse to consent" to a pet [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The provider is taken to have consented unless, within 14 days of receiving the request, they apply to the Tribunal for an order that it is reasonable to refuse [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- On such an application, the Tribunal may consider the type of pet, the character of the premises, the appliances and fittings, whether refusal is permitted under any Act, prescribed matters, and any other relevant matter [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Allergy is not listed. The Tribunal may also order that the pet is permitted [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What this means for you**

1. **Timing is key.** Your request was sent about three weeks ago. If the owner did not apply to the Tribunal within 14 days of receiving it, the law treats consent as given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). An agent's refusal does not, by itself, change that. Check whether any VCAT application was filed and when.
2. **If the refusal was made in time and no Tribunal application was filed,** you can point out that the owner is taken to have consented under s 71C(2) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **If a Tribunal application was filed,** the Tribunal decides whether refusal is reasonable, and the outcome is not determined by the documents. The owner's rarely visiting may be relevant to the "character and nature" of the arrangement, but the documents do not say how the Tribunal would weigh an allergy or a visit pattern.
4. **Don't move the dog in yet** unless you have written consent or a Tribunal order, because keeping a pet without either breaches s 71A [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If a pet is excluded by Tribunal order, the provider may later give a notice to vacate if you don't comply [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. For advice, the Regulations list Victoria Legal Aid on 1300 792 387 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover**

- Whether an owner's allergy is a "reasonable" ground for refusal.
- Whether the agent's refusal counts as the owner's refusal for these purposes.
- Whether a Tribunal application was made, which you'll need to check.

**Documents relied on**

- [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf, dated 13 October 2026, Authorised Version 115 (in force on 15 October 2026).
- [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf, dated 30 June 2026, Version 009.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered: the 14-day rule ('The provider is taken to have consented unless, within 14 days of receiving the request, they apply to the Tribunal'), its application to the three-week timeline ('Your request was sent about three weeks ago. If the owner did not apply to the Tribunal within 14 days of receiving it, the law treats consent as given'), and a next step ('Check whether any VCAT application was filed and when').

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer avoids all three fail conditions: it does not treat the agent's refusal as final ("An agent's refusal does not, by itself, change that"), it places the Tribunal application on the owner rather than the renter ("unless, within 14 days of receiving the request, they apply to the Tribunal"), and it does not say the allergy automatically decides the matter ("Whether the refusal is reasonable is not something the documents resolve for an allergy").

Its only other source is the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 "Version 009", dated 30 June 2026 (link 21-3sra009), also the in-force version, and no rule comes from any other version.

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the retrieved law, yes. The notice to vacate stays in effect unless it is formally withdrawn, and the buyer pulling out does not withdraw it by itself. The landlord also still has to go through VCAT before you can be forced out.

The version in force on 1 October 2025 is the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (No. 109 of 1997), Authorised Version **v110**, which applies from 6 August 2025 to 24 November 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

### What the law says

- **Sale notices:** A landlord may give a notice to vacate if the premises are, immediately after the termination date, to be "sold or offered for sale with vacant possession." The notice must give at least 60 days' notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Withdrawal:** A notice to vacate "is withdrawn only if a notice of withdrawal is given." That withdrawal must be in writing, signed by the person who gave the notice, and signed by the person it was given to [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). A landlord's change of plans is not, on its own, a withdrawal.
- **Possession orders:** If the landlord applies to VCAT for a possession order, VCAT must be satisfied that the notice "has not been withdrawn" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **No self-help eviction:** A landlord must not require or compel you to leave, or enter the premises to take possession, except as the Act allows. The penalty is 150 penalty units for a natural person or 750 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do or ask

1. **Check the notice's validity.** A sale notice is only valid if it is in the prescribed form, is addressed to you, is signed, gives the reasons, includes the required documentary evidence approved by the Director, and states the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
2. **Challenge it at VCAT if it is defective.** You can apply to VCAT challenging the notice's validity, but the application must be made within 30 days after the notice was given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Check when you received it, because that deadline may already have passed.
3. **Ask the landlord to withdraw it in writing.** A withdrawal only takes effect if both you and the landlord sign it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
4. **Wait for any VCAT application.** If the landlord applies for a possession order, you can attend and argue the notice is not valid or was not properly withdrawn or relied on. You should not move out simply because the sale fell through, unless you have signed a withdrawal or VCAT orders it.

### What the documents don't cover

- The retrieved documents don't say whether a sale notice automatically lapses when the sale falls through. The statutory ground refers to premises being sold or offered for sale immediately after the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Whether that condition is still met after the buyer withdrew is a question for VCAT, and the documents don't resolve it.
- I don't have the date the notice was served, so I can't tell whether the 30-day challenge window is still open.

**Next step:** Contact Consumer Affairs Victoria on 1300 558 181 or a community legal centre for advice on your specific notice [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). This is general information, not legal advice.

must-mention.reason: No: the answer misses the first point. It never says the outcome depends on the ground stated in the notice and its supporting evidence, such as a planned sale with vacant possession versus a signed contract. It quotes 'sold or offered for sale with vacant possession' and mentions documentary evidence, but it gives a flat 'yes' rather than tying the answer to which ground and evidence the notice relied on. The other points are covered: 60 days, withdrawal in writing signed by both, and the VCAT challenge within 30 days or asking for a written withdrawal.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the three failure conditions is asserted: the answer says "the buyer pulling out does not withdraw it by itself," requires withdrawal to be "signed by the person who gave the notice, and signed by the person it was given to," and states the notice "must give at least 60 days' notice."

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
**Short answer:** Under the documents, a rent increase is only valid if you received a proper written notice. Your agent's email and the failed negotiation don't appear to meet that requirement, so you probably don't have to pay the higher rent yet. The documents don't say exactly what an email must contain to count, so check this with Consumer Affairs Victoria.

Both documents below were in force on 1 October 2025.

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997**, Authorised Version (version 110), in force from 6 August 2025 to 24 November 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021**, Authorised Version (version 004), in force from 1 July 2025 to 24 November 2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

### What the law says

- The rental provider "must give a renter at least 60 days notice in the prescribed form of a proposed rent increase" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The notice must state the amount of the increase, the method used to calculate it, and your right to apply to the Director within 30 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- A notice can provide for only one increase [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- Rent cannot be increased at intervals of less than 12 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- "A rent increase in contravention of this section is invalid" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The prescribed form is Form 5, which says "A valid notice of a proposed rent increase is required for all rent increases" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do

1. **Ask for a formal notice.** Ask the agent or owner to send a notice in the Form 5 format. Check that it gives at least 60 days' notice, states the amount and calculation method, and includes the 30-day review statement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
2. **Check the timing.** If a valid notice is given, the increase cannot start until at least 60 days after notice. You should also check whether the rent has already been increased in the last 12 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
3. **Ask Consumer Affairs Victoria to review it.** If you think the proposed rent is excessive, you can apply to the Director in writing within 30 days after the notice is given. This is free [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
4. **Apply to VCAT if needed.** You can apply to VCAT within 30 days after receiving the Director's report, or within 30 days after the notice is given if there is no report. However, Form 5 warns that "You will need to pay the increased rent amount from the date provided on this notice unless VCAT decides otherwise" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**From when?** If there is no valid notice, the documents indicate the increase is invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If a valid notice is later given, the documents only say it must give at least 60 days' notice. They do not set a specific start date beyond that.

For further information, Form 5 lists Consumer Affairs Victoria on 1300 558 181 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). This is general information, not legal advice.

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
**Short answer:** Not quietly. The Act requires you to tell the owner in writing about the damage, and it doesn't cover insurance.

**Version applied:** As at 15 October 2026, the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 is *rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf*, which the document metadata gives as version 115 and in force from 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 is *rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf*, version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

---

### What the law says

- **Damage is the renter's responsibility.** A renter and their visitors must not intentionally or negligently damage the rented premises. Fair wear and tear is excluded [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A dog chewing skirting boards is likely to count as damage, though whether it was negligent is a factual question the documents don't resolve.
- **You must notify the owner.** A renter who becomes aware of damage must give written notice as soon as practicable, stating that the damage occurred and its nature [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Notice can be given electronically [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Repairs by you are restricted.** The regulations' summary says only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, both urgent and non-urgent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs don't appear to apply.** A renter can arrange urgent repairs only after taking reasonable steps to have the owner do them immediately and being unable to get that done [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). "Urgent repairs" is a defined list [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't list chewed skirting boards, so this route probably doesn't fit.
- **The owner can require you to repair it.** If the owner gives a written repair notice for damage caused by your breach, you have 14 days to repair it in a proper and tradesman-like manner. If you don't, the owner may do the repairs at your expense [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You must reimburse reasonable repair costs within 14 days after they're completed, if the owner gives written particulars of the cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The bond can cover it.** The owner can claim from the bond the reasonable cost of repairing damage caused by the renter, taking fair wear and tear into account [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What the renter can do or ask

1. **Give written notice now.** Describe the damage (chewed skirting boards) and send it in writing, by email if the owner agrees to electronic notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Offer to have it fixed before you leave.** Ask the owner whether they want you to arrange repairs, and get the quote in writing. Any work should be done by a suitably qualified person [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Ask for written agreement on cost.** If the owner accepts your repair or a cost deduction from the bond, record that agreement in writing. The documents don't set out a specific procedure for this, so keep the paperwork.
4. **Expect the end-of-tenancy inspection.** The owner must complete the final inspection and fill in the condition report within 10 days after the end date, and allow for fair wear and tear [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

Doing repairs without telling the owner would not remove the written-notice duty [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). It could also leave you with a bond claim or a repair-notice dispute.

### Insurance

The documents I retrieved don't address the owner's insurance or whether this damage would affect a policy. You should ask the owner or check the policy directly. Insurance is outside what these sources cover.

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't say how many circuits a rental must have. The specific electrical rule starts after your date, but you can still ask your landlord for safety checks and repairs under existing duties.

**What the law says on 1 March 2023**

- The applicable regulations are the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version No. 002, incorporating amendments as at 1 June 2022 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The Act is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, version 101, in force from 7 September 2022 to 23 May 2023 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- The circuit rule is in Schedule 4, clause 9. It says that "On and from 29 March 2023," all power outlets and lighting circuits must be connected to a switchboard-type circuit breaker complying with AS/NZS 3000 and a switchboard-type residual current device [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Because 29 March 2023 is after 1 March 2023, this rule is not yet in force on your date.
- A rental provider must ensure the premises comply with the rental minimum standards on or before the day the renter moves in [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) (s 65A(1)). They must also provide and maintain the premises "in good repair" and "in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) (s 68(1)).
- Electrical safety checks must be done "every 2 years by a licensed or registered electrician," and the provider must give the date of the most recent check in writing on request [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf) (Schedule 3, clause 1).

**What you can ask for**

1. **Safety check records:** Ask in writing for the date of the most recent electrical safety check [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The provider must give you a copy of the most recent check within 7 days of a written request [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf) (regulation 30(2)(c)). If no check has been done in the last 2 years when you moved in, the provider must arrange one "as soon as practicable" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
2. **A repair:** You must give the provider written notice "as soon as practicable" after becoming aware of damage or a breakdown of facilities or equipment they provided [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) (s 72AA). Repairs must be done by "a suitably qualified person" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) (s 68(4)).
3. **If they don't act:** For non-urgent repairs, you can apply to the Director to investigate if repairs aren't done within 14 days of your written notice [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) (s 74). You can also apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) (s 75).
4. **Urgent repairs:** You may arrange urgent repairs if you have taken reasonable steps to get the provider to do them immediately and they haven't [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) (s 72(1)). The provider must reimburse reasonable costs up to $2500 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The documents list urgent repairs as including failure of essential services or appliances for "hot water, cooking, heating or laundering" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). They do not mention power circuits, so I can't confirm whether a tripping breaker counts as urgent.

**Heater note:** Until 28 March 2023, a fixed heater in good working order must be in the main living area [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf) (Schedule 4, clause 14). The energy-efficient heater requirement starts 29 March 2023 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover**

- The required number of circuits.
- Whether a breaker that trips under load breaches any standard on 1 March 2023.

For guidance, the documents point to consumer.vic.gov.au/renting [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). A licensed electrician can also check whether the wiring is overloaded.

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. The answer says "The documents don't say how many circuits a rental must have," which counts as stating that no rule exists. For next steps, it says to "Ask in writing for the date of the most recent electrical safety check" and to give "written notice" requesting a repair, with an urgent-repair option.

The answer states "The documents don't say how many circuits a rental must have" and that the circuit breaker/RCD rule applies "On and from 29 March 2023" and so "is not yet in force on your date," so it asserts neither a minimum number of circuits nor that the standard already applies.

The answer names the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 as 'Authorised Version No. 002, incorporating amendments as at 1 June 2022' (link 21-3sra002) and the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as 'version 101, in force from 7 September 2022 to 23 May 2023' (link 97-109aa101), both in force on 1 March 2023, and all applied rules come from these versions (the 29 March 2023 circuit rule is in version 002 itself and is correctly described as not yet in force).

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I found don't say whether coin-operated washing machines can be charged for. They do set rules for charges and for laundry facilities generally.

**What the law says**

- **Charges must be scheduled and itemised.** If a rooming house operator charges for services, the operator must give you a separate schedule of those charges before you move in, and if you use a service, an itemised account of your individual use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Utility charges have a specific rule.** An operator may charge for electricity, gas and water used in a room only if the operator pays the bill and the room is separately metered. The charge must not exceed what the supplier charges [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This section doesn't clearly cover laundry machines, so I can't say it applies to them.
- **Homes Victoria and registered housing agencies are different.** They may impose a service charge for laundry or utility services only in a declared rooming house, and only where it isn't possible or practicable to measure your use accurately. The charge must not exceed the cost of providing the service [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This applies only if your operator is one of these bodies.
- **Unreasonable limits on utilities are prohibited.** A rooming house agreement cannot contain a term that unreasonably limits your use of utilities [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Laundry standard.** From 26 February 2024, laundry facilities must include a washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether those machines must be free.

**What you can do or ask**

1. Check your agreement and house rules for a schedule of services and any laundry charges. Ask the operator for this schedule if you don't have it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. Ask for an itemised account of what you've been charged for laundry use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. If the operator is Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency, ask whether the charge is a service charge under the rules above. You can apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (the Tribunal) for an order to withdraw or vary it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. If the charge seems unreasonable or the coin machines are the only option, you may wish to get advice from Victoria Legal Aid or Consumer Affairs Victoria. The documents don't cover this, so I can't confirm their role.

**Versions used:** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 is at Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026, which applies on 15 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 are at Version No. 009 (in force from 30 June 2026) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), and the Rooming House Standards Regulations 2023 are at Version No. 002 (in force from 1 December 2024) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf).

All four points are present: the output says 'laundry facilities must include a washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents'; states 'The documents don't say whether those machines must be free'; notes the operator 'must give you a separate schedule of those charges before you move in'; and advises to 'Check your agreement and house rules for a schedule of services... Ask the operator for this schedule if you don't have it.'

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't say whether a listing may show mould. A photo is good evidence that mould may be present, but the documents don't say whether it is enough to prove a breach of the minimum standards. The versions in force on 1 October 2025 are the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 004 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf), and the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**What the law says**

- **The mould standard:** The mould standard I found is in Schedule 6, which applies to community housing or housing provided under a specialised housing program. It says "each room in the rented premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). I could not find the equivalent standard for ordinary private rentals in the retrieved documents, so I can't confirm it applies to this property.
- **Duty to comply:** A rental provider must ensure the premises comply with the rental minimum standards on or before the day the renter moves in [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The provider must also keep the premises in good repair and reasonably fit for occupation [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Advertising:** The Act lets a provider enter to take advertising images or video, but only after notice, and the renter can object to images showing their possessions [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). These rules cover taking the photos, not what a listing may show. I found no provision that bars advertising a visible defect.
- **Disclosure to applicants:** The regulations require the provider to tell a rental applicant whether the premises comply with the rental minimum standards, and whether they have received a repair notice in the last 3 years relating to mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure (on and from 31 December 2021) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). This is the closest rule to the advertising question, and it applies to what the provider tells applicants.

**Is the photo enough?**

The documents don't say what evidence is needed or how much weight a photo carries at VCAT. A photo can show that mould appears to be present, but the standard also requires the mould to be "caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). A photo may not show the cause. The documents don't answer whether a photo alone would be enough.

**What the renter can do or ask**

- **Ask for disclosure:** Ask the provider in writing whether the premises comply with the rental minimum standards and whether there has been a mould or damp repair notice in the last 3 years [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Before moving in:** A renter may terminate a residential rental agreement before taking possession if the premises do not meet the rental minimum standards, by giving notice on that ground [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **After moving in:** The renter may issue a request for urgent repairs if the premises do not comply on or immediately after the occupation day [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The renter must notify the provider in writing of damage and of breakdowns as soon as practicable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). The renter can apply to VCAT for an order requiring non-urgent repairs if they have not been done within 14 days of notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Gather evidence:** The documents don't say what evidence VCAT requires. Dated photos, written notices, and any reply from the provider would be useful, but I can't confirm from these documents that they will be sufficient.

I'd recommend checking the current general rental minimum standards and VCAT's evidence requirements, since those aren't in the documents I retrieved.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
I'm assuming you are the renter and that your friend moved in without the landlord's written consent. The retrieved documents don't say whether a friend moving in counts as "sub-letting" without a payment or formal arrangement.

**Which law applies:** The *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (title "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (title "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", Authorised Version No. 009, in force from 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) were both in force on 15 October 2026.

## What the law says

- **Consent is required.** A renter "must not assign or sub-let the whole or any part of the rented premises without the residential rental provider's written consent" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Unconsented arrangements are invalid.** An assignment or sub-letting without consent "is invalid unless the Tribunal has determined that consent is not required" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The landlord can end your tenancy.** The provider "may give a notice to vacate rented premises if the renter has assigned or sub-let or purported to assign or sub-let the whole or any part of the premises without the residential rental provider's consent." The notice "must specify a termination date that is not less than 14 days after the date on which the notice is given" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations say the same [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **The landlord cannot unreasonably refuse consent**, and cannot charge a fee for it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Under the Act, the provider "must not demand or receive a fee or payment for giving consent," and doing so carries a penalty of 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

- **Ask for written consent now.** The provider "must not unreasonably withhold consent" to sub-letting [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Your request should be in writing, and you should not offer or pay a fee for consent.
- **If consent is refused,** you may apply to VCAT "for a determination that the consent … is not required" if you believe the refusal is unreasonable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Expect a possible notice to vacate.** If the landlord does not consent, they can give you a notice to vacate with at least 14 days before the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You can challenge the notice at VCAT, for example if you believe it was not given properly [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Getting your friend out.** The documents don't say how a renter can remove a non-renter occupant. What they do say is that the landlord can't personally use force to remove a tenant. Only Victoria Police can carry out a forcible eviction, and only on a VCAT order (warrant for possession) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Your friend is not a party to the agreement, and the documents don't cover how a notice works against them.

## What the documents don't cover

- Any notice or process to remove an occupant who is not a renter, beyond the VCAT process above.

question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?

- **Challenging a notice:** A tenant who has received a notice to vacate under ss 255–260, 285, 286 or 310 may apply to the Tribunal challenging its validity, within 30 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (ss 321B, 321C). Section 263 is not in that list [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Possession orders:** The Tribunal must make a possession order if the landlord was entitled to give the notice and it has not been withdrawn [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 330(1)(a)). It cannot determine the application before the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 329).
- **Retaliation:** The contents list shows "s 266 – Notice to have no effect in certain circumstances," but the text of s 266 is not in the retrieved pages. The retrieved text only shows retaliation-type rules for other tenancy types, such as rooming houses [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 142ZA(3)). If it cites another ground, the 30-day route applies.

3. **Your repair requests.** Note the dates and whether each was in writing, because non-urgent repair rights depend on written notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 74(1)).
4. **Whether the landlord withdrew the notice.** A notice is withdrawn only by a written notice of withdrawal, signed by both the person who gave it and the person it was given to [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 321).

The Tribunal can decide whether the notice is valid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 321C(1)). If it finds the notice valid, you cannot apply again unless "exceptional circumstances" exist [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 321C(2)).
- **Ask for urgent repairs.** You may arrange them if you have taken reasonable steps to get the landlord to repair immediately and you cannot get them done [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 72(1)). You must give the landlord 14 days' written notice of the repairs and cost. The landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost or $1000, whichever is less [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 72(2)). question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved law gives you possible grounds to challenge the rental provider's conduct, mainly for the rent-auction and misleading-conduct rules. It does not say whether an email "withdrawal" you didn't make is binding, so I can't confirm that part.

**Version applied:** Today is 1 October 2025, so I used the versions in force on that date. The *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* is version 110, in force from 6 August 2025 to 24 November 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* is version 004, in force from 1 July 2025 to 24 November 2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

### What the law says

- **Advertised rent must be a fixed amount.** A provider or agent must not advertise or offer premises unless the rent is advertised or offered as a fixed amount. The maximum penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person or 300 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **No soliciting higher offers.** A provider or agent "must not solicit or otherwise invite an offer of an amount of rent that is higher than the advertised amount of rent." The same penalties apply [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). This is the most relevant rule if the agent invited the higher offer. The documents don't say whether simply accepting an unsolicited higher offer breaches this rule.
- **No false or misleading rent advertising.** A provider or agent must not make a false or misleading representation about rent in promoting or advertising premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **No misleading conduct to induce an agreement.** A provider or agent must not induce a person to enter a residential rental agreement by misleading or deceptive conduct. This applies to providers not acting in trade or commerce, and the penalties are the same as above [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Section 472(1A) provides for Tribunal orders for contraventions of this section [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Discrimination.** A provider must not refuse to let premises on a protected attribute [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The Statement of Information for Rental Applicants says that if a provider or agent has unlawfully discriminated against you and you suffered loss, you may apply to VCAT for compensation under section 210AA [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

### What the documents don't cover

- Whether an email withdrawal you did not send is valid, or how a withdrawal should be recorded.
- Whether a rent increase after you applied is lawful in itself.
- Any specific evidence rules for rental applications. The condition-report rules in the documents relate to the start and end of a tenancy, not applications [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do

1. **Seek advice.** Victoria Legal Aid can be called on 1300 792 387 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
2. **Apply to VCAT** if you suffered loss from a contravention of these provisions. VCAT can be contacted at vcat.vic.gov.au or on 1300 018 228 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
3. **Complain about discrimination** if the reason for the decision was a protected attribute. You can contact VEOHRC at humanrightscommission.vic.gov.au or on 1300 292 153 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

### What to save as evidence

The documents don't list evidence requirements for this situation. The following is general practical advice, not drawn from the documents:

- The original advertisement, including the advertised rent, with screenshots and the date.
- Your application and any confirmation of it.
- The withdrawal email, with full headers, and any follow-up messages.
- Any messages in which you said you had not withdrawn.
- Records of the new listing and its rent, with dated screenshots.
- Anything showing what the agent said about other offers or higher bids.
- Records of any loss you incurred, such as costs of searching or moving.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not. Under the Act as it stands on 15 October 2026, the agent may refuse only if it is reasonable to do so, and the 14-day window to challenge your request may already have closed.

## What the law says

- The governing document is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). That version was in force on 15 October 2026.
- A renter may keep a pet if the provider has consented in writing or the Tribunal has ordered it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- A renter's request must be made in the form approved by the Director, and given to the provider [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Since you used the official form, this requirement appears to be met.
- The provider **must not unreasonably refuse** consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The provider is **taken to have consented** unless, within 14 days after being given the request, the provider applies to the Tribunal (VCAT) for an order that refusal is reasonable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The Regulations' standard residential rental agreement form repeats this: the rental provider "must not unreasonably refuse a request to keep a pet" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). That document is the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## Applying this to your situation

- **Deemed consent:** Your request was made about three weeks ago, so roughly 24 September 2026. The 14-day window would have closed around 8 October 2026. If the agent did not apply to VCAT by then, the owner is taken to have consented [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Check the exact date you gave the request, and whether any VCAT application has been filed.
- **Reasonableness:** The documents do not say whether an owner's allergy is a reasonable ground for refusal. The Tribunal, if asked, may consider the type of pet, the character of the premises and fittings, and "any other matter the Tribunal considers relevant" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents do not say how an allergy that rarely affects the owner would be weighed.

## What you can do

1. **Get the refusal in writing** if you have not already, and note the date you sent the request and the date the agent refused.
2. **Confirm whether an application was lodged** with VCAT within 14 days of your request [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If none was, you can point to deemed consent in your reply.
3. **Ask the agent or owner in writing** to confirm that the pet is approved, and state that the provider is taken to have consented under the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Seek advice or apply to VCAT** if the provider disputes this. The Tribunal can decide whether refusal is reasonable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Risk to note:** If the Tribunal later excludes the pet, you could face a notice to vacate if you do not comply with the order after at least 14 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The documents do not cover the owner's allergy specifically, or how VCAT would decide a dispute over it. For that, you would need to check VCAT's guidance or get legal advice.

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the retrieved documents, the notice is still in effect unless the landlord formally withdraws it. The documents don't say whether a notice to vacate for a sale lapses when the sale falls through, so you should get advice on that point.

## What the law says

- **The notice stays valid until it is formally withdrawn.** A notice to vacate "is withdrawn only if a notice of withdrawal is given." The withdrawal must be in writing, signed by the person who gave the notice, and signed by the person to whom it was given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). A landlord's decision not to sell, or the buyer pulling out, does not by itself withdraw the notice under this section.
- **The sale ground.** A landlord may give a notice to vacate if the premises are, immediately after the termination date, "to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession." The termination date must be **not less than 60 days** after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Form requirements.** A notice to vacate is not valid unless it is in the relevant prescribed form, addressed to the renter, signed, states the reason, and, for sale notices, is accompanied by documentary evidence approved by the Director [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The prescribed form is Form 6 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Timing for sale notices.** If a contract of sale is conditional, the landlord may give the notice within 14 days after the last condition is satisfied. If the contract is not conditional, the notice must be given within 14 days after the contract is entered into [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## What the renter can do or ask

1. **Ask for the withdrawal in writing.** If you want certainty, ask the landlord to sign a formal notice of withdrawal that meets the requirements above [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Do not assume the notice is gone without it.
2. **Check the notice's validity.** Look at the termination date (at least 60 days after the notice was given), the form, the signature, the stated reason, and whether the documentary evidence was attached [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). The renter can apply to VCAT challenging the notice's validity within **30 days after the notice to vacate is given** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). I don't know when your notice was given, so check this deadline now.
3. **Leave early if you wish, with no lease break fee.** A renter who has been given a notice to vacate under this section can give a notice of intention to vacate with a termination date **not less than 14 days** after the notice is given. A renter who does this is not liable for any lease break fee [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
4. **Wait for any possession application.** If you do not leave, the landlord may apply to VCAT for a possession order. VCAT decides whether the landlord was entitled to give the notice and whether you must leave and on what date. Only Victoria Police can carry out a forcible eviction, and only under a VCAT warrant [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
5. **Get advice.** The Form 6 information sheet recommends seeking advice immediately if you may have grounds to challenge the notice, through community legal organisations or Consumer Affairs Victoria (1300 558 181) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

The retrieved documents don't say whether a sale-based notice to vacate remains enforceable after the sale collapses. They also don't cover whether a landlord must withdraw it in that case. Those questions need specialist advice or a VCAT decision.

**Sources:** Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110 (in force 6 August 2025 to 24 November 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 004 (in force 1 July 2025 to 24 November 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Both were in force on 1 October 2025.

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the retrieved documents, probably not. A rent increase needs a valid written notice, and an email saying the rent is going up is unlikely to meet that requirement. The documents don't say when the higher rent would start without such a notice.

**Versions in force on 1 October 2025:** The *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Version 110, in force from 6 August 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (Version 004, in force from 1 July 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) both apply on that date.

### What the law says

- **Notice is required:** A rental provider "must give a renter at least 60 days notice in the prescribed form of a proposed rent increase" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Prescribed form:** The regulations provide Form 5, and state that "A valid notice of a proposed rent increase is required for all rent increases" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Invalid increases:** "A rent increase in contravention of this section is invalid" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Timing limit:** Rent cannot be increased at intervals of less than 12 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Fixed terms:** During a fixed term, rent can only rise if the agreement provides for it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do or ask

1. **Ask for the formal notice.** Request a Form 5 notice. It must state the current and new rent, the start date, and the method used to calculate the increase, and it must name the rental provider (not the agent) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
2. **Check the start date.** A valid notice must give at least 60 days' notice, so any start date must be at least 60 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
3. **Challenge it if it is excessive.** You can apply in writing to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria within 30 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). You can also apply to VCAT within 30 days after the Director's report, or within 30 days after the notice where there is no report [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
4. **Expect to pay if VCAT does not intervene.** Form 5 says you will need to pay the increased amount from the date on the notice unless VCAT decides otherwise [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

### What the documents don't cover

- **Whether an email could ever count as notice:** The documents require the prescribed form, but they don't address edge cases such as an email that includes the required details.
- **Your specific start date:** Without a valid notice, I can't identify a date from these documents.
- **Your agreement's terms:** I don't know whether you're on a fixed term or periodic agreement, or when your last rent increase took effect.

This is general information from the legislation, not legal advice. If you're unsure, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria.

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
**Applicable versions (as at 15 October 2026):** The *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* reprint, version 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The retrieved documents give version numbers, not "Authorised Version" numbers as such, so I've used those.

## What the law says

- **Damage:** A renter and their visitors must not intentionally or negligently cause damage to the rented premises. Fair wear and tear doesn't count as damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Your dog chewing the skirting boards would likely be damage, not fair wear and tear.
- **Notice:** A renter who becomes aware of damage must, as soon as practicable, give the provider written notice of the fact that the damage occurred and its nature [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Notice can be given electronically [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Who can do repairs:** Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, whether urgent or non-urgent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Repair notice:** If damage results from the renter's failure to comply with the duty not to damage the premises, the provider may give a written repair notice. The renter can then repair it within 14 days in a tradesman-like manner. If they don't, the provider may repair it at the renter's expense [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Your liability for costs:** The renter is liable for the reasonable cost of repairs the provider undertakes, if the provider gives written particulars of the cost. The renter must reimburse within 14 days after the repairs are completed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **End of tenancy:** The renter must leave the premises in the same condition as when they moved in, taking fair wear and tear into account [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Can you get it fixed quickly without telling the owner?

**No, not as a way around notice.** The law requires written notice of the damage as soon as practicable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Skirting board damage is unlikely to be "urgent repairs" under the Act's definition, which covers things like burst water services, gas leaks, and faults making premises unsafe or insecure [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). So the urgent-repair route, which lets a renter arrange repairs and claim reimbursement, probably doesn't apply. For non-urgent repairs, the renter must notify the provider in writing and the provider must carry out repairs in a reasonable time [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do:**
1. Give the owner or agent written notice of the damage now, describing what happened and where [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Email is acceptable if the agreement allows electronic service [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. Offer to have a suitably qualified person repair it, and ask whether the owner wants to arrange it or have you arrange it. Get written agreement before you do any work [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. If the owner doesn't repair it, you can apply to the Director to investigate if repairs are not done within 14 days of your written notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Note that the Director's process is for non-urgent repairs and the documents don't say what happens with damage caused by the renter.
4. Keep receipts and photos, since the Act lets the tribunal consider whether the renter gave written notice and whether documentary evidence of repairs was provided [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't cover whether the owner must accept your repair choice, or the exact steps for a renter who repairs damage they caused, beyond the repair notice process above [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Would it affect the owner's insurance?

**The documents don't say.** The retrieved material covers the Act and the Regulations only, and nothing addresses insurance policies or how property damage claims interact with them. You'd need to check the owner's policy or ask the owner or agent directly.
