question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't set a minimum number of circuits. The circuit-breaker and safety-switch rule exists, but it doesn't start until 29 March 2023, after today's date. The documents don't say what applied before that.

Applicable versions: Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, version 002 (in force 1 June 2022 to 30 November 2024) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf), and Residential Tenancies Act 1997, version 101 (in force 7 September 2022 to 23 May 2023) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Electrical standard:** "On and from 29 March 2023," all power outlets and lighting circuits must be connected to a switchboard-type circuit breaker complying with AS/NZS 3000, and a switchboard-type residual current device complying with one of the listed standards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The clause doesn't say how many circuits a rental must have [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Timing:** Because this applies from 29 March 2023, it isn't in force on 1 March 2023 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Minimum standards:** The provider must ensure the rental meets the rental minimum standards on or before the day you move in [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The provider must also keep the premises "in good repair" and "in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Electrical safety checks:** The provider must ensure an electrical safety check is done every 2 years by a licensed or registered electrician. If no check has been done in the last 2 years when you move in, the provider must arrange one "as soon as practicable" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Who can do repairs:** Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, urgent or non-urgent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The Act says the same for repairs and maintenance [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

## What you can ask for

1. **Safety check records:** Ask in writing for the date of the most recent electrical safety check. On written request, the provider must give you a copy of the most recent check within 7 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
2. **An electrical inspection and repair:** Ask in writing for a licensed or registered electrician to inspect the circuits and fix the fault. Under the Act, any repair must be done by a suitably qualified person [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Written notice:** Notify the provider in writing of the fault as soon as practicable. For non-urgent repairs, the provider must carry them out within a reasonable time. You can apply to VCAT if they aren't done within 14 days of notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Urgent repairs (possibly):** Urgent repairs include failure of an essential service or appliance for cooking or heating [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether a tripping breaker counts. If it does, the provider must carry out urgent repairs after notice. If you arrange them after taking reasonable steps, you can be reimbursed for the reasonable cost up to $2,500 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
5. **Heating:** A fixed heater in good working order must be in the main living area of a Class 1 building [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If the heater is tripping the circuit, that's a fault to report.

If the fault creates an immediate danger, stop using the affected circuit and tell the provider in writing straight away. The condition report guidance says to tell the provider about "any defect that could be a threat to safety" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't clearly say whether a private rooming house operator can charge for coin-operated washing machines. The Act has specific charging rules, but none expressly covers laundry charges by private operators.

**What the law says**

As at 15 October 2026, the applicable version is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, version 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

- **Separately metered rooms:** An operator may charge for electricity, gas and water consumed in the room, but only if the operator pays those utilities, the room is separately metered, and the charge is no more than the supplier's charge [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This does not cover laundry.
- **Services charges:** If an operator charges for services, it must give the resident a separate schedule of those charges before the resident moves in. If the resident uses a service, the operator must provide an itemised account of that individual use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Service charges by public housing bodies:** Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency may impose a service charge for laundry or other services in a declared rooming house, but only if it is not possible or practicable to measure the resident's use accurately. The charge must not exceed the cost of providing the service [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This power is limited to those bodies, so it does not explain a charge set by a private operator.
- **Washing machines must be provided:** From 26 February 2024, the standard for laundry facilities is a washing machine for every 12 or fewer residents, based on the house's maximum occupancy [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). The retrieved version of the Rooming House Standards is version 002, in force from 1 December 2024 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Ask the operator for the charging basis in writing.** Ask whether the machines are a charged service and, if so, for the separate schedule of charges that the operator must provide before you moved in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask for itemised accounts** if you are charged for using the machines [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Check who runs the house.** If Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency imposes the charge, you can ask the Tribunal to order it withdrawn or varied, and the charge must be notified to you in writing [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Ask about the washing machine provision.** If the house does not have a washing machine for every 12 or fewer residents, that may breach the standard [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). The documents do not say what remedy applies to that breach.
5. **If a fault causes excess usage charges,** the operator may be liable, but only if you notified the operator as soon as practicable and the fault was not caused by you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The documents I retrieved do not say whether a private operator may charge coin-operated laundry fees, or how such fees must be set. For that, you would need to check the house rules and your residency agreement, or seek advice from the Tribunal or a tenancy service.

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't say whether a provider may show mould in an ad. They do set a mould standard, but they don't say a photo alone proves a breach. The renter can ask for repairs, report the problem, or end the agreement if they've not yet moved in.

**Which law applies:** On 1 October 2025, the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Authorised Version No. 110, in force from 6 August 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (Authorised Version No. 004, in force from 1 July 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) were both in force.

### What the law says

**The mould standard.** Schedule 4 provides that "each room in the rented premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Mould in a bedroom therefore falls under this standard if it is caused by or related to the building structure.

**Advertising.** The Act says a provider or agent must not make a false or misleading representation about the characteristics of the premises [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). It also covers advertising images: a provider may enter to produce advertising photos or video after giving notice [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The documents do not say whether showing mould in an ad is permitted, or what the ad must say about it.

**Whether the photo proves the breach.** The documents don't say a photo is conclusive. A condition report signed by both parties is conclusive evidence of the state of repair on the day it records [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), but this is a different document from an ad photo. The regulations say photos "may be useful in a dispute about the condition of the rented premises" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Whether a photo is enough in a particular case is not addressed in the retrieved documents.

**Duty to comply.** A provider must ensure rented premises comply with the rental minimum standards on or before the day the renter moves in [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

### What the renter can do or ask

- **Ask for the mould to be fixed.** A renter can request urgent repairs if the premises don't comply with the minimum standards on or just after move-in [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). "Urgent repairs" include "a failure to comply with any rental minimum standards" and "the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **End the agreement before moving in.** A renter who hasn't taken possession can give notice ending the agreement on the ground that the premises "do not meet any rental minimum standards" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Ask for a condition report and photos.** Before moving in, the provider must give a condition report, and the renter can add comments and photos [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Renters should take dated photos of the condition, including at the start of the tenancy [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Seek a dispute outcome.** The regulations say that where repairs aren't done within a reasonable time, a renter can apply to VCAT for an order requiring them [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

### What the documents don't cover

- Whether the ad itself was lawful, and what wording or disclosure would be needed.
- Whether a photo, without an inspection or repair notice, is enough evidence that the mould breaches the standard.
- The meaning of "caused by or related to the building structure" in a specific case.

For those questions, you would need guidance from Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT, which aren't in the retrieved material.

- **Unauthorised sub-letting is invalid.** An assignment or sub-letting without consent is invalid unless the Tribunal has determined that consent is not required [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Notice to vacate.** A provider may give a notice to vacate if the renter has assigned or sub-let, or purported to assign or sub-let, without consent. The prescribed form is Form 6 in the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Possession order.** If the renter stays past the termination date, the provider may apply to the Tribunal for a possession order. That application must be made no later than 30 days after the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal must make the order only if it is satisfied of the statutory conditions and that the order is reasonable and proportionate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
**Short answer:** Under the Act as it stands on 15 October 2026, the owner cannot simply refuse because of an allergy. - The Act is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). That is the version in force on your date.

- The provider **must not unreasonably refuse** consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The provider is **taken to have consented** unless, within 14 days after being given the request, they apply to the Tribunal [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- To refuse, the provider must apply to the Tribunal for an order that it is reasonable to refuse consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A refusal by the agent alone does not appear in the documents as a way to stop deemed consent.

Allergy is not mentioned specifically.
- The Regulations' standard agreement form repeats that the provider "must not unreasonably refuse a request to keep a pet" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). That document is the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the retrieved documents, a notice to vacate stays in effect unless it is formally withdrawn, and the buyer pulling out does not withdraw it by itself. The documents do not say whether a sale-based notice remains valid once the sale has fallen through, so you should get advice on that point.

**Applicable law:** The *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version (version) 110, was in force from 6 August 2025 to 24 November 2025, which covers 1 October 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 004, was in force from 1 July 2025 to 24 November 2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**What the law says about your situation:**

- **Basis for the notice:** A landlord may give a notice to vacate if the premises are to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession immediately after the termination date. The termination date must be at least 60 days after the notice is given [1, s 91ZZB(1), (4)]. If a contract of sale is conditional, the landlord may give the notice within 14 days after the last condition is satisfied [1, s 91ZZB(2)].
- **Withdrawal:** A notice to vacate "is withdrawn only if a notice of withdrawal is given." That notice must be in writing and signed by both the person who gave the notice and the person it was given to [1, s 91ZZQ]. Because the landlord has not withdrawn it, the notice has not been withdrawn under this rule.
- **Possession orders:** If you do not leave, the landlord may apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) for a possession order. The Tribunal must be satisfied that the notice "has not been withdrawn" [1, s 330(1)(a)(ii)]. The Tribunal also must consider whether a possession order is reasonable and proportionate [1, s 330(1)(f)].
- **Validity:** The notice must be in the prescribed form, addressed to you, signed, state the reasons, and state the termination date [1, s 91ZZO]. For a sale notice, it must also be accompanied by documentary evidence supporting the reason [1, s 91ZZO(e)]. Note that a notice must be in the "relevant prescribed form" [1, s 91ZZO(a)]. The Form 6 notice tells renters that a notice can be challenged if, for example, "it was not given to you properly" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask:**

1. **Check the timing to challenge.** You may apply to VCAT challenging the validity of the notice. The application must be made within 30 days after the notice is given [1, s 91ZZS]. question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
**Short answer:** Not unless you received a valid written notice. An email saying the rent is going up, followed by a refused negotiation, does not appear to meet the legal requirements. The documents don't say what happens if the agent later gives a proper notice, so I can't give a start date for a rent increase that hasn't been properly notified.

I've relied on two versions in force on 1 October 2025: the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Authorised Version No. 110, in force from 6 August 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (Authorised Version No. 004, in force from 1 July 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**What the law says**

- A rental provider must give at least 60 days' notice, in the prescribed form, of a proposed rent increase [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The notice may provide for only one rent increase, and must state the amount of the increase, how it was calculated, and your right to apply to the Director within 30 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The prescribed form is Form 5, and it states that "A valid notice of a proposed rent increase is required for all rent increases" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- Rent can't be increased at intervals of less than 12 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- A rent increase made in breach of these rules is invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

- **Ask for the formal notice.** Request a written notice in the Form 5 format. It must name the rental provider (not the agent), state the current and new rent, the start date, and the calculation method [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Check the timing.** If the notice gives less than 60 days, or increases the rent less than 12 months after the last increase, it may be invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Apply for a review if you think the rent is excessive.** You may apply in writing to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria within 30 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). The form says the request can be posted to GPO Box 123 Melbourne 3001 or emailed to renting@justice.vic.gov.au [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Apply to VCAT.** After the Director's report, you may apply to VCAT within 30 days of receiving it. If you don't request a report, you can apply directly to VCAT within 30 days of the notice, though you may need to show reasonable grounds [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Note the payment rule.** Form 5 warns that you will need to pay the increased amount from the start date on the notice unless VCAT decides otherwise [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). So the 30-day deadlines matter.

**What the documents don't cover**

- They don't say whether an informal email or a verbal statement from an agent has any legal effect beyond being an invalid notice. They also don't say what date an increase would take effect if a valid notice were served late or defectively.
- They don't cover your specific tenancy, such as whether it's a fixed-term agreement, the rent amount, or when your last increase was. If you're in a fixed term, the rent can't be increased before the term ends unless the agreement allows it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

If you tell me your lease type and when the rent last changed, I can check those points against the documents.

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
**Short answer:** No. The law expects you to tell the owner in writing about the damage, and generally only a suitably qualified person may do repairs. The documents I found don't say whether the damage affects the owner's insurance.

I've applied the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, version 115 (in force from 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, version 009 (in force from 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Both were in force on 15 October 2026.

### What the law says

- **Damage by a renter:** A renter and any visitor must not intentionally or negligently cause damage to the rented premises. Fair wear and tear is excluded [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Whether chewing by a dog counts as negligent damage depends on the facts, and the documents don't address pets causing damage.
- **Written notice is required:** A renter who becomes aware of damage must, as soon as practicable, give the owner written notice of the fact that the damage occurred and its nature [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Notice can be given electronically [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Who can do repairs:** Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, both urgent and non-urgent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Renter-arranged repairs are limited to urgent repairs:** A renter may arrange urgent repairs only if they have taken reasonable steps to get the owner to do them immediately, and the owner hasn't [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). "Urgent repairs" is a defined list that covers things like burst water service, gas leaks, dangerous electrical faults, and faults that make premises unsafe or insecure [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Chewed skirting boards probably don't fall within that list, so this route is unlikely to apply. Check with the Consumer Affairs Victoria guidance if unsure.
- **The owner can choose to have you repair it:** If damage is caused by the renter's failure to take care, the owner can give a written repair notice requiring you to repair it at your expense within 14 days, in a tradesman-like manner. The owner can also undertake the repairs and charge you the reasonable cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If you don't comply, the owner can apply to the Tribunal [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do or ask

1. **Don't do the repair secretly.** Give the owner or agent written notice of the damage and its nature now [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This is what the law requires, and it lets you choose a path with them.
2. **Offer to have a suitably qualified person repair it,** and ask the owner to confirm in writing whether they want you to repair it or will arrange it themselves [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Get quotes and keep receipts.
3. **Check the end-of-tenancy process.** The owner must complete the final inspection and fill in the condition report within 10 days after the agreement ends, and must allow for fair wear and tear [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). You are also required to leave the premises, as far as practicable, reasonably clean and in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Take dated photos** of the damage and any repair, as the regulations recommend photos for disputes about condition [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

### Insurance

The documents I retrieved don't address whether the damage or any repair affects the owner's insurance policy. You should ask the owner or check the policy terms directly.

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I retrieved don't set a minimum number of circuits or say how many power points a rental must share. They do contain electrical safety rules and a duty to meet the rental minimum standards, and your situation may fall under those. The electrical circuit-breaker rule takes effect after your date, so on 1 March 2023 it isn't yet in force.

**What the law says**

- **Rental minimum standards:** On and from 29 March 2023, all power outlets and lighting circuits must be connected to a switchboard-type circuit breaker that complies with AS/NZS 3000 "Electrical Installations," plus a switchboard-type residual current device meeting one of the listed standards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). This is in the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (version 002), Schedule 4, clause 9 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Because 1 March 2023 is before 29 March 2023, this rule is not yet in force on your date. The documents don't say how many circuits are needed.
- **Duty to comply with the standards:** A provider must ensure the rented premises comply with the rental minimum standards on or before the day the renter moves in [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). This is section 65A(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Authorised Version No. 101) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The Regulations prescribe these standards in Schedule 4 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Duty to maintain:** The provider must keep the premises "in good repair" and "in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) (section 68(1), Act Version No. 101).
- **Electrical safety checks:** The provider must ensure an electrical safety check of all electrical installations, appliances and fittings they provided is done every 2 years by a licensed or registered electrician. On request, they must give the date of the most recent check in writing [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf) (Regulations, Schedule 3, clause 1). If no check has been done in the last 2 years when you move in, the provider must arrange one as soon as practicable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

**What you can ask for**

1. **Ask for a written electrical safety check.** You can request the date of the most recent check in writing [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If the check is more than 2 years old, the provider must arrange one as soon as practicable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask for repairs in writing.** Report the problem to the provider in writing as soon as practicable, since the Act requires written notice of damage or breakdown of facilities [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) (section 72AA). Describe the tripping and which appliances cause it.
3. **Urgent repairs (if they apply).** A renter may arrange urgent repairs only if they have taken reasonable steps to get the provider to do them immediately and the provider is unable to get the repairs done [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) (section 72(1)). The documents don't say whether a tripping breaker counts as an urgent repair, so check the definition in section 3(1) of the Act, which I did not retrieve.
4. **Non-urgent repairs.** If the repair isn't urgent, you can give written notice, and if the provider hasn't acted within 14 days, you can apply to the Director to investigate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) (section 74(1)).
5. **Tribunal orders.** You may apply to VCAT for an order requiring specified repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) (section 75(1)).

**What I couldn't confirm:** Whether a shared circuit breaks the minimum standards, or whether your breaker tripping shows a fault, is not in the documents. An electrician should assess the wiring and load. The documents also don't cover any rule on the number of circuits in a rental.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I found don't say whether a rooming house operator can charge for coin-operated washing machines. They do set rules for any service charges an operator imposes, and those rules may apply to you.

**Version applied:** The *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026) is the version in force on 15 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations and Standards documents I found are not the same instrument, and I cite them only where relevant.

**What the law says**

- **Utility charges:** An operator may charge for electricity, gas and water only if the operator pays for them, the room is separately metered, and the charge is no more than the supplier's charge [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Nothing in these provisions covers coin-operated machines.
- **Service charges:** If an operator charges for services, it must give you a separate schedule of those charges before you take up residency. If you use a service, it must give you an itemised account of your individual use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Homes Victoria and registered housing agencies:** Section 109A allows a service charge for laundry or utility services, but only where Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency runs the house, and only if use can't practicably be measured. The charge must not exceed the cost of providing the service [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This likely doesn't apply to a private operator.
- **Facilities:** Operators must keep facilities in good repair [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), and must give residents access to other facilities during all reasonable hours [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Laundry standard:** From 26 February 2024, a rooming house must provide a washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). The standard doesn't mention charging.

**What you can do or ask**

1. Ask the operator for the written schedule of services that should have been given to you before you moved in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Check whether the washing machine charge is listed.
2. If you are charged, ask for an itemised account of your individual use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. If you are charged for a fault-related excess (for example, a leak), the operator may be liable for the extra cost, and you must notify it as soon as practicable [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Either you or the operator can apply to the Tribunal about excessive usage charges [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. If a machine is broken, report it to the operator [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). You can arrange urgent repairs in some circumstances [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't cover whether a coin-operated machine counts as a "service" that can be charged for, or how to dispute a machine charge beyond the excessive-usage process. For that, you may need to check the Act's full text or seek advice from a tenancy service.

**References**
[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Version 115 (in force from 2026-10-13), ss 108, 109, 109A.
[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Version 115 (in force from 2026-10-13), ss 120, 120AA, 120AAB, 129.
[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf) Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023, Version 002 (in force from 2024-12-01), reg 14.

It notes that service charges require 'a separate schedule of those charges before you take up residency'. It advises the reader to 'Ask the operator for the written schedule of services that should have been given to you before you moved in'.

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't say whether a rental ad may show mould. They do say the rental provider must disclose certain mould information to applicants and must keep rooms free of mould. The photo alone probably isn't enough to prove a breach, because the documents don't address how such a breach is proven. Both laws in force on 1 October 2025 are the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (version 004, in force 1 July 2025 to 24 November 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) and the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (version 110, in force 6 August 2025 to 24 November 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**What the law says**

- **The standard:** Each room must be "free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Timing:** The provider must ensure the premises comply with the rental minimum standards on or before the day the renter moves in [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repair:** Mould or damp "caused by or related to the building structure" is listed as a fault that can be an urgent repair [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**Can they advertise it like that?**

The documents don't address whether an ad may show mould. The Act's advertising provision (s 89A) covers only the provider's right to enter a occupied property to take advertising images, and the renter's right to object to images that show their possessions [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). It says nothing about how a defect must be described.

The documents do require disclosure to applicants. The provider must give the applicant:
- whether the premises comply with the rental minimum standards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
- whether, in the last 3 years, the provider has received a repair notice relating to mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure (from 31 December 2021) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

The documents don't say what evidence is needed or whether a photo is sufficient. They also don't say how a dispute about mould would be decided. Some points to consider:
- The standard covers only mould or damp "caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). A photo shows mould, but not its cause.
- A photo doesn't show when it was taken or whether the mould was present when the renter moved in.

**What the renter can do or ask**

- **Ask for the disclosures above** in writing before signing, including whether the premises comply with the minimum standards and whether there has been a mould-related repair notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Notify the provider in writing.** The renter must notify the provider in writing "as soon as practicable" of damage, and the provider must carry out non-urgent repairs "in a reasonable time." The renter may apply to VCAT if repairs aren't done within 14 days of notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repair route:** If the mould is caused by the building structure, the renter can ask for an urgent repair [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If the provider doesn't carry it out after being notified, the renter may arrange repairs and be reimbursed "up to $2500," or apply to VCAT [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Before moving in:** A renter who hasn't taken possession may give a termination notice on the ground that the premises "do not meet any rental minimum standards" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't set out a process for a renter to remove a friend who is living in the property. They do show that letting someone move in without the landlord's written consent is a breach that can lead to a notice to vacate for you, the renter. The documents don't say whether a friend living there without paying rent counts as "sub-letting," so that needs checking.

## What the law says

- **Consent is required.** A renter "must not assign or sub-let the whole or any part of the rented premises without the residential rental provider's written consent" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Regulation 27 says the same thing [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Unauthorised arrangements are invalid.** An assignment or sub-letting without consent "is invalid unless the Tribunal has determined that consent is not required" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The landlord can't unreasonably refuse consent.** A residential rental provider "must not unreasonably withhold consent" to sub-letting [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Notice to vacate.** A landlord may give a notice to vacate if the renter "has assigned or sub-let or purported to assign or sub-let" without consent. The termination date must be "not less than 14 days after the date on which the notice is given" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Regulation 27 also says the landlord "may give the renter notice to vacate" in this situation [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Form of notice.** A notice to vacate is not valid unless it is in the prescribed form, addressed to the renter, signed by the person giving it, states the reasons, and specifies the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Entry.** The landlord or agent may enter if they have "reasonable grounds to believe that the renter has failed to comply with the renter's duties" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Challenging the notice.** The 30-day right to apply to VCAT to challenge a notice applies to notices under sections 91ZX, 91ZY, 91ZZ, 91ZZA, 91ZZB and 91ZZC, not to a notice for unauthorised sub-letting [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Regardless, the Act says nothing in that Subdivision "affects any right a renter may have to challenge the validity of any other notice to vacate" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Withdrawal.** A notice to vacate is withdrawn "only if a notice of withdrawal is given," and it must be signed by both the person who gave the notice and the person it was given to [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

1. **Talk to the agent or landlord now.** Under the Act, consent can't be unreasonably withheld [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), so you could ask for consent for your friend to stay. This may be the cleaner route if the friend is staying long-term.
2. **If you want your friend to leave,** the documents don't set out a renter's power to remove an occupant. Ending the arrangement is a private matter between you and your friend. Your obligations under the agreement continue while they are there, including the duty not to cause damage or nuisance [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Expect possible consequences.** If the agent finds out, they may give you a notice to vacate with at least 14 days' notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). They may also enter the property if they have reasonable grounds to believe you have breached your duties [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Get advice.** Consumer Affairs Victoria can be reached on 1300 558 181, and community legal organisations are listed on its website [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**Gaps in the documents:** They don't define "sub-let" or say whether a friend staying without paying rent is covered. They also don't set out a renter's process for removing a non-tenant occupant. The definitions section and any rules on occupants were not among the retrieved text, so I can't confirm them.

Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, version 009 (in force from 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Both were in force on 15 October 2026.
